passage.title: The Vault at the Top of the World
paras: Far to the north, on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard islands, a narrow concrete entrance pokes out of a frozen mountainside. There is almost nothing else to see: snow, rock and, for months of the year, darkness. Yet behind that door lies one of the most precious stores on Earth.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened in 2008. Its job is simple to describe and vital to do: it keeps copies of the seeds of the world's food crops. If a disaster such as a flood, a war or a disease destroys a country's own seed bank, that country can ask for its seeds back and start again.

Why build it here? The mountain rock is deep and stable, and the ground stays frozen all year. Inside, the seeds are kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius, sealed in packets and stored in boxes on long metal shelves. Even if the electricity failed, the permafrost around the vault would keep the seeds cold for a long time. The vault is also high above the sea, so it should stay dry even if ice melts and sea levels rise.

More than a million samples are stored there, from rice and wheat to beans and barley, sent by countries all over the world. Each country still owns the seeds it deposits; Norway simply looks after them, free of charge.

The vault has already proved its worth. In 2015, scientists whose seed bank in Syria had been damaged by war withdrew seeds from Svalbard, grew them in other countries, and later sent new seeds back to be stored again.
Some people call it the 'doomsday vault'. Its builders prefer a gentler idea: a safety deposit box for farming, so that the crops which feed us are never lost for good.

questions.q: When did the seed vault open?

questions.a: Copies of the seeds of the world's food crops

questions.q: Give two disasters that could destroy a seed bank.
At what temperature are the seeds kept?

questions.a: Sealed in packets, in boxes on long metal shelves

questions.q: What would keep the seeds cold if the electricity failed?
Why was it built high above the sea?
questions.a: To stay dry even if ice melts and sea levels rise

questions.q: About how many samples are stored?

questions.a: Nothing: it is free of charge

questions.q: Which country's scientists withdrew seeds in 2015?
Find and copy a word that means 'very important'.
Why does the writer describe the entrance as 'narrow' and the surroundings as empty?
questions.a: To contrast the plain outside with the precious store inside, making the vault seem surprising and secret

questions.q: Explain why Svalbard is a good place for the vault. Give two reasons with evidence.
questions.a: Deep, stable rock and ground frozen all year; high above the sea so it stays dry

questions.q: How does the 2015 example show the vault has 'proved its worth'?
questions.a: Syria's war-damaged seed bank could restart by withdrawing seeds, growing them and sending new seeds back

questions.q: Why do the builders prefer the idea of a 'safety deposit box' to the 'doomsday vault'?
questions.a: It sounds calm and practical, about keeping something safe, rather than frightening and about the end of the world

questions.q: Summarise the passage in one sentence.
questions.a: In the frozen Arctic, the Svalbard vault safely stores copies of the world's crop seeds so that farming can recover from any disaster.
